text:
And then there’s the situationship, which is hard to define because that’s basically the point. Usually it’s a happenstance relationship based on sex. There’s less communication, and what communication exists is more superficial. Yet it is obviously some kind of relationship even while one or both people refuse to name it. You’re regularly having sex, going out together, spending time alone together, and doing things you wouldn’t do with a regular friend, so it feels like it’s filling a relationship void, but only accidentally and occasionally—maybe just enough to keep you from looking for anything deeper.

It can go either way, but often the man wants to keep it undefined while the woman wants commitment, partly because she’s the one risking pregnancy. Whoever keeps it undefined gets the fun without the responsibility. People still get pregnant and attached, though, whether or not anybody named the relationship, and the one keeping it undefined still ends up with the existential void another superficial fix creates. Doomscrolling entertains you too.

And “Why are you making this heavy?” can be a real question. They may actually mean: don’t you want the fun, and are you about to give it up? My answer would be: I’m trying to understand whether this is really fulfilling me or if it’s drainingly superficial.

I had something sort of like that with H., although ours was much deeper than what people normally mean by situationship. We were (and still are) BFFs, and spent nearly all our time together. She was falling in love with me, and I wasn’t falling in love with her. She felt more like a sister to me, partly because I’m not attracted to white women. Ours wasn’t superficial, just painfully uneven.
reader: Someone in a relationship that is mostly sex and has no name, deciding whether to ask what it is.

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")? (E375)
question_text.Q5: Why does each sentence follow from the one before? (every but, so, because and this has what it turns on)
question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
question_text.Q7: Does each fact help this reader now, in their case (the same kind of thing they face, not just the same topic)?
question_text.Q8: Does each item belong in the group it is put in?
question_text.Q9: Is anything compressed? (one step a sentence, the small words that carry the relation, no space before mg)
